utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] I'm starting over again. I would like to welcome everybody in the courtroom, the accused, I would also like to welcome the Defence counsel, as well as members of the OTP, and everybody who is helping us in these proceedings. We are continuing today with the closing arguments. General Praljak will have exactly 30 minutes. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor for your 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I extend my greetings to everybody in the courtroom. I especially extend my greetings to the interpreters. Your Honours, the training of police officers from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia, who were sent by the SDA as early as 1991, the training of pilots of the BH Army in the Republic of Croatia, the training and equipping of entire BH Army units in Croatia, the taking up of hundreds of thousands of Muslim refugees in Croatia, the organisation of ex-territorial education and schooling for Muslim refugees in the Republic of Croatia in the Bosnian language, which at the time didn't even exist, the uninterrupted supply of weapons to the BH Army, ammunition, oil, medication, food, and other necessary logistics for the BH Army in order to wage a war, the medical treatment of more than 10.000 wounded BH Army combatants in Croatian hospitals, enabling thousands of Mujahedin to come and join the BH Army, regular logistic bases of the BH Army in Zagreb, Rijeka, Split, Samobor, throughout the war, and so on and so forth, and all of this for free, never in the history of war has one people, the Croats, provided so much help to another people, the Bosnian Muslims, even when the latter turned their army, the BH Army, against the Croats, the HVO, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Never in the history of war has the commander of one army, the HVO, let convoys with armaments and other equipment pass through to another army, the BH Army, even when that army, the BH Army, used those armaments and all the rest to attack those who let them receive it. And what about the referendum of Croats for Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was a precondition for the existence of that state, the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Republic of Croatia, the appointment of the ambassador of the Republic Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the signing of all propositions made by the international community on the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the first ones to sign were the representatives of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Croatia. That was the policy of Dr. Franjo Tudjman, president of the Republic of Croatia. It was the policy of the Government of Croatia, the Parliament of Croatia and the Ministry of Defence of Croatia. It was the policy of the HVO. To the Prosecution of this Tribunal, all these are elements of a joint criminal enterprise. Such an indictment uses logic that is offensive even to the cognitive system of a pathogenic virus. What kind of opinion and which positions precede such an indictment? Firstly, Simon Leach, a former police constable in Great Britain, member of the OTP team who investigated crimes committed by Croats in the Lasva Valley, at some meeting in the Prosecution in 1996, produced a piece of paper with names, the names of Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak and Vice Vukojevic. He interpreted and explained that these were the goals that his investigation was led to. Secondly, I quote from Willem Montgomery's book, "After the Cheering Stops," page 114: "The US special ambassador for war crimes, Pierre Prosper, invited three American ambassadors from the region, from Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia to come to The Hague in order to meet with the representatives of the ICTY. There are two memories rather impressive. The first one refers to the fact that we heard directly from Carla Del Ponte that the official approach of her office is based on the position that all war leaders of all parties are guilty of war crimes, and, further on, that she considers which these specific crimes are and how their guilt can be proved. At that moment, it seemed, and it still seems to me, that such a position is false for several reasons." Is Mr. Montgomery a credible witness? What was the reaction of the other three? The positions of Carla Del Ponte are not false for many reasons. Her position is imperial arrogance, a degradation of law and its reduction to Communist purges and Nazi pogroms. Thirdly, in her book "La Caccia: Io e Il Criminali Di Guerra," Carla Del Ponte says, on page 254: "One of the Prosecutors of the Tribunal, a Canadian, well known in his circle for his wit and anecdotes, had an aphorism that did a good job capturing the difference between the Serbs and the Croats who attempted to obstruct the work of the Tribunal. The Serbs are bastards, he used to say. In contrast, the Croats are perfidious bastards." This Prosecutor of the Tribunal, the Canadian, is using hate speech. Del Ponte uses the phrase "he used to say," which means that it was not a one-off witty remark, but a habitual chauvinistic and racist characterisation of the Croats as perfidious bastards. Carla Del Ponte relays the words of one of the Prosecutors of the Tribunal without any restrictions, which means that she completely agrees with that opinion; on an ongoing basis, too, which we can infer from the language and the phrase "he used to say." The lack of any reaction to such a pro-fascist manner of speech about one nation is something I cannot comprehend. I'm interested to know whether the indictment against me may have been drafted under the impression of such an opinion. If, by any chance, I, Slobodan Praljak, had written or said anything like that, anywhere, at any time, about any people or nation or group during the war in the territories of the former Yugoslavia, I would have been sentenced to five years of imprisonment only for that. I really would like to know whether the saying "quod licet Iovi, non licet bovi" is something that is a valid rule here in this Tribunal. I really would like to know whether the international organisations, which established the Tribunal and which ensure that it is fair, support the position mentioned in the book, this book. The Prosecution has compared me to the Nazis and my activity to the Holocaust. Well, let me then describe the role of Goering, which character, according to the Prosecution, I compare. This Goering placed his Jews - actually Muslims - in his country cottage and took care of them. He put his Jews in his apartment in Zagreb. He fed them and gave them medical treatment. He exposed himself to sniper fire in front of the JNA barracks at Grabovina in order to save the wives of his enemies. He protected the captured JNA soldiers with his own body and saw to it that they make it to their homes safe and sound. He pulled out captured Serb civilians from the Dretelj Camp, although he was being threatened with weapons; not alone, though. The camp was held by HOS members, who were mostly Muslims. He evacuated wounded Jews - actually Muslims - from the hospital in East Mostar; not alone, of course. He organised the evacuation and accommodation of 15.000 Jews - actually Muslims - from Stolac and the Dubrava Plateau, across the Neretva, and 3.000 of their cars. He didn't do that alone, either. He transported a wounded Jewish women - actually Muslim woman - by helicopter from East Mostar to split; not alone. He received a Jewish - actually Muslim - family with a child suffering from leukemia near Uskoplje and transported them to Split to be treated. He helped them to get Croatian citizenship in order to travel to Switzerland and be treated medically at the expense of the Croatian state budget; not alone, though. He organised that the Salvation Road for Jews - actually Muslims - be built in order to be able to leave to another country, Goering's country, Croatia. He didn't do it alone, though. He guided them and fought with the Jews - actually Muslims - defending and liberating Mostar and Capljina and Travnik and Konjic and other places. He didn't do that alone either. He, of his own accord, let the captured Jews - actually Muslims - go who were captured after the conflict in Rama or Prozor, and he prevented retaliation after the Jews - actually Muslims - committed crimes in Uzdol. He didn't do that alone, and the same applies to Doljani and Grabovica. When necessary, he personally let through convoys transporting food for the Jews - actually Muslims - as well as convoys with armaments, even when the 3rd Corps of the BH Army, the 4th Corps of the BH Army, the 6th Corps of the BH Army and parts of the 1st Corps of the BH Army launched an attack against Goering, against the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the port of Ploce, after they had signed a truce with the Serbs. He didn't do that alone either, and so on and so forth. I'll skip Goering's - that is Praljak's - behaviour in the courtroom, but that behaviour makes one a war criminal according to the logic applied by the OTP. The Prosecutor quoted Goethe's Faust about the mirror that we should look -- that you would use to look at ourselves. My actus reus are my mirror, my point and my very essence, because they follow from the mens rea of that one who we call Slobodan Praljak. Unfortunately, Judges Prandler and Trechsel refused to accept my 150 witnesses who were supposed to testify about the activities and deeds of the accused Praljak, and about the general situation in which such deeds were necessary, but, unfortunately, not always sufficient, and I really fail to understand the legal procedure that forbids me to testify about Mladic's diaries. Do I regret the victims? Yes, I regret all innocent victims of all war. I especially regrets the victim of those 500 wars or so after 1945 that have taken place and still go on, despite all moralists' speeches that we hear daily. I especially regret every child that, in reality, dies of hunger every four seconds. Peace in dictatorship is a preparation for war. The longer and the worst the dictatorship, the more negative energy builds up and the more blood and evil will follow later. It doesn't matter whether we're talking about Tito or Saddam. And those who bring down a dictator and who later try to diminish the evil that occurs according to the force of the laws of physics, but those who made possible the dictatorship and by their silence made it last longer. The same applies to Yugoslavia after Tito as well as to Iraq after Saddam. What the Prosecutor calls nationalist is something the Croats felt a necessity for freedom, both the freedom of the people and citizens' freedom. In this sense, I am a Croatian nationalist. I do not renounce the policy of Dr. Franjo Tudjman because that policy created the Republic of Croatia and made possible the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state. I do not renounce the inherent sense and point in the legal establishment of the HZ-HB, the expression of the will of the Croats in BH to become and remain a sovereign and constitutive people in that state. The HZ-HB, by its frail organisational structure, made possible the creation of the HVO, which in 1992 was able to defend the BH and the south of Croatia in 1993, prevented the implementation of the aggressive plans of the BH Army. The Muslim policy and the BH Army, unable to regain the territories that were occupied by the JNA and the VRS, and that was due, to a large extent, to the weapons embargo that is incomprehensible to an ethical human mind, moved to launch a counter-offensive against the HVO. By liberating areas from Croats, they committed crimes at Konjic, Capljina, Doljani, Bugojno, Grabovica, Uzdol, and elsewhere. The facts are plain to see for the killed, expelled and detained Croats. Social relations are an area where the laws of cause and consequence apply, whereas the spiral of evil, once initiated, does not justify crime, but it does significantly reduce the possibility to implement the law, whoever's task that is on paper. It is always like that, and everywhere. The HVO defended itself from an aggression in 1992, in 1993, and 1994, and a commander's duty is not to lose the war. My conscience is clear. Legal proceedings are the interpretation of laws and facts in a trial proceedings, as rhetoric, and, as such, does not seek to find the absolute truth. It seeks to find a probable truth beyond all reasonable doubt, which can be contradicted hardly or not at all. In an attempt to discover such truth, knowledge is not enough. One needs to ponder, one needs to apply logic, one needs to apply rational and logical argumentation, data, facts, statements, and statistics do not mean a thing if they are not in a logical relationship with assertions. Through connecting various types of knowledge can we get closer to the truth. In these proceedings, one requires knowledge from the field of sociology, sociology of war, knowledge about societies in which state and social structures are completely destroyed, in which individuals return to their natural state. One needs to apply knowledge from the field of war psychology as well as the knowledge of war skills, armament, and the understanding of the real term of the military, and so on and so forth. Possible mistakes in the interpretation of facts are probable and just as well fatal. Exaggerated and false reduction of terms and of logical connections, making conclusions on the basis of false presumptions, avoiding comparing similar systems and phenomena, arbitrary equalising of terms "power" and "desire," which is so dear to intellectuals, arbitrary accusations because the world is not how one wishes or conceives it to be, these are all fields of possible logical errors in the final assessment of facts. I sincerely hope that the honourable Trial Chamber will adhere to scientific methods and notions. In the last century, millions of people were convicted in trial proceedings pursuant to racial laws, for example, in the USA and Pretoria, dictatorial, religious and Nazi laws in Germany, Serbia, Slovakia, the independent state of Croatia, fascist laws which were applicable in Italy, Communist laws which were applicable in the former Soviet Union and Yugoslavia, and so on and so forth. The court rhetoric has been under the influence of unreasonable social and political powers for too long, and that is why it has been criticised; unfortunately, not loudly enough. In order to not end up in moral desperateness, it is high time for it to become what it has to be, a moral and reasonable process. Do I have the right to hope? I would kindly ask the honourable Judge Antonetti to tell me how much more time I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you please confirm the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Enough. Laws of this Tribunal may be what they are. However, they do not apply to the Americans. For other peoples, laws of the Permanent Court apply, and those laws again differ from the laws applied here at the ICTY, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, laws which are applied to me. This abolishes a significant condition of the court rhetoric, which is the principle of the equality of arms among the participants in the trial proceedings. And now I quote Perelman: "In a relation where inequality is a significant and characteristic of relations among people, there is no foundation for a reasonable and judicious process." And for the end, I'm not guilty, and I'm not referring here to the feeling of guilt, coldly, rationally, with a logical analysis that has been critically examined dozens of times. I know I'm not guilty. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, if your judgement is the opposite of my conclusion, I will respect the general principle of challenging every opinion, conclusion, or attitude. I shall reconsider my position on my own responsibility openly and courageously. If I recognise a mistake after that, I shall serve my time because you are righteous. I will know what I could have done better, how I could have done it better, where I could have done it better, and when I could have done things better, in my thoughts and in my words, in what I did and in what I failed to do. If, however, you do not convince me and if your interpretation of facts is not a good-enough or a falsely application of sum of social sciences, and what is not possible thus becomes possible, what is not simple thus becomes simple, and the power to do something thus becomes just a substitute for a desire or a wish, then I will be in jail only because the Tribunal is might, and this wouldn't be anything new under the sun, really. My half hour is finished. I would like to thank you for your attention now and over the past several years. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'm going to give the floor to the Petkovic Defence, who are, I believe, prepared. So I'm giving the floor to Ms. Alaburic, who will present the argumentation on behalf of the Petkovic Defence. I am reminding her of her time, which is five hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. Good afternoon to my learned friends from the OTP, the accused, the other counsel, and all of those who are with us at the moment. On behalf of the General Petkovic Defence, I'm going to present our closing argument. I will be the only one to speak. I have my co-counsel, Zoran Ivanisevic, who is currently in Zagreb, and we have a new member of the team, Mr. Guenael Mettraux, who is our legal consultant. On the screen, you can now see the title page, and you can see who members of the Petkovic Defence team are. They all participated in the preparation of our closing argument. Before I start my closing argument, I have to use the magic word "Sanction" to launch the presentation that we have prepared for you, Your Honours. And before I start, I would kindly ask my associate to distribute the binders that we have prepared for the Trial Chamber. We would kindly ask the assistance of the Usher. Your Honours, we have the hard copy of our presentation for your benefit to allow you to follow us and to check all those things that we will be presenting, that we will try to explain to you. The Powerpoint presentation is also in e-form, so if any of the parties in these proceedings is interested in obtaining the electronic form, you can address the case manager of the Petkovic team and you will be provided with an electronic version of our presentation. And now I'm starting the closing argument on behalf of the Petkovic Defence. Your Honours, certain crimes were, indeed, committed in the area of Herceg-Bosna. Crimes should not be forgotten. Victims have the right to receive justice. Perpetrators must be punished, and accused have the right to a fair trial. A fair trial is one of the basic human rights. Human right to a fair trial includes, inter alia, an obligation of the Judges to rely only and exclusively on evidence heard in the courtroom and to establish the facts only and exclusively on the evidence in the case. Victims of a crime have a legitimate interest in participating in any proceedings against an accused. The ICTY Statute, unfortunately, does not provide such a possibility, like the ICC Statute. The Prosecutor's invitation to Judges to think about the victims and to listen to the voices of victims is not an invitation to a fair trial, in our opinion, for at least three reasons. The first one: Judges in a criminal proceedings are not expected to protect victims, but rather to decide about the criminal responsibility of the accused. Secondly, Judges are not supposed to rely on the voices of anybody outside the courtroom. And, thirdly, Judges are not supposed to rely on anything other but the evidence in the case. The goddess of justice is blind, because the Tribunal has to be impartial. Judges must not harbour preconceived notions about the matter put before them. Judges have to decide the case exclusively on the basis of their reasonable assessment of the evidence and the application of the law. Your Honours, I believe that we have a consensus in this courtroom on these principles, and I'm mentioning just in response to the Prosecutor's appeal for you to listen to the voices of the victims that we did not hear in this courtroom. The Petkovic Defence will talk about victims in its final argument. We will mention certain numbers in relation to the victims. When we mention numbers, there is always a feeling of discomfort, because a crime against one person is no less terrible than a crime against 10 people. We will not mention the figures to diminish or minimise the victims' suffering or the consequences of the crime. Numbers are supposed to help us understand the essence of the case. Let's start with some general data about the crime bases. The table in front of you is based on paragraph 229 of the indictment. Out of the crime bases, we have singled out the crime of persecution because the underlying act of that is a different crime, and we believe that if you look at all the other crimes, you will gain a good insight into the structure of the crime base. The Prosecutor compiled his indictment for a total of 903 crimes barring the Prosecution. The majority of the crimes is relative to inhumane acts, accounting for about 25 per cent. What follows are crimes of incarceration, with a share of 20 per cent. The total share of crimes relative to incarceration, and we're talking about bullet points 10 through 18, is about 54 per cent. If we look at the crimes of deportation and transfer together, they make up about 20 per cent. And if we add up all of the crimes that we have just mentioned, namely, deportation, transfers, and crimes relative to imprisonment, pertaining to bullet point 6 to 18, we will see that approximately three-fourths of the total crime base is relative to the aforementioned crimes. If you look at the table, you will see that certain crimes have been marked in red. Let us remember these crimes. These crimes, according to the Prosecutor's final argument, make up an element of the JCE from the 1st of July, 1993. Those are crimes which make up the JCE Forms 1 and 2, both detention and deportation, again from the 1st of July, 1993. I would like to draw your attention, Your Honours, to the fact that there are no charges for attacking undefended towns, villages, residential and other facilities. Killings, Your Honours, is most commonly the essence of war, and it is one -- the ratio is 1:10 at the expense of civilians. Let's analyse the killing and murder charges in this case. The next table refers to killings, murders, and unlawful killings as presented in the indictment. All of the columns contain a reference to a paragraph in the indictment and the number of victims as presented in the indictment. The total number of killed has been segregated into four different groups. The first group is made up of those who were killed during combat or after combat. The second are those who were alleged human shields at the moment when they died. The third group is composed of those who were killed during an alleged unlawful labour. And the fourth group are those which, according to the Prosecutor, died during the imprisonment. Let's look at the first column, those who died during or in relation to combat. Out of the total number of victims which we could find in the indictment, and that is 242, 103 victims died during combat or immediately after combat or in relation to combat. Therefore, less than one half of those victims were killed during or in relation to combat. On the following 10 pages, Your Honours, we have prepared for you a brief analysis of all the pieces of evidence that the Prosecutor presented in Annex A of his final brief, and all of them are in respect of murder, willful killing, and I don't intend to analyse every piece of evidence at the moment. My learned friend from the Prosecution will be provided with this analysis in an electronic form to be able to check the veracity of our claims, but let me just present the results of our analysis. Paragraph 48 of the indictment, the village of Paljike. Our analysis indicates that the Prosecutor did not prove that there had been murder committed there. In paragraph 51, we see the village of Toscanica. Our analysis indicates that the Prosecutor failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the crime of murder had been committed. Paragraph 66, the village of Dusa. Having analysed the evidence, we conclude that the Prosecutor failed to prove the committed acts of murder, although it is not disputed that a certain number of civilians were killed during the attack on the village by the HVO. Paragraph 66, the village of Hrasnica. The Prosecutor failed to prove that the crime of murder of civilians was committed. Paragraph 77, the village of Sovici. The evidence suggests that the killed persons were "hors de combat," and they are not a legitimate target of attack, as such, which means that the Prosecutor did prove that the crime of murder was committed. Paragraph 114 has to do with shelling and sniping in Mostar. We analysed the evidence of until the 24th of July, 1993, and we established that the Prosecutor proved the murder of one victim, Arzemina Alihodzic. And in Annex A, we find no evidence on the victims of shelling which could be seen as the victims of the crime of murder. Paragraph 161. Our analysis indicates that the Prosecutor proved that the crime of murder was committed on Sanida Kaplan. Paragraph 176, Domanovici. Our analysis indicates that the Prosecutor managed to prove that the crime of murder was committed. Paragraph 177, the village of Bivolje Brdo. Our analysis indicates that the Prosecutor proved that the crime of murder was committed, and the victim was Hasan Korac. However, the Prosecutor did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the crime of murder was committed against the 12 victims referred to in that paragraph. Had we had sufficient number of pages and sufficient word count for our final brief, we would have conducted a similar analysis as per each charge of the indictment. Unfortunately, we had an insufficient number of pages, so we needed to focus only on matters which were of importance for General Petkovic's Defence. What was our aim in stating all this? The Prosecution, in its final trial brief, stated that the crimes of murders and willful killings were not planned by the HVO or in the context of JCE, that these crimes were not part of the criminal common plan. The Petkovic Defence agrees that the crimes of murder and willful killing of Muslims and Bosniaks in Herceg-Bosna were not part of some criminal common plan or a means to persecute the Muslim Bosniak population. In other words, Your Honour, the aim of the Armed Forces of Herceg-Bosna was not to kill the Muslim population. Given that the chief of the Main Staff is part of the military authorities, this fact alone is of crucial importance for the Defence of General Petkovic. The continuation of our closing argument, Your Honours, will be dedicated to the topic of the joint criminal enterprise. We will spend significant time on that topic; I believe up to an hour. To start with, by your leave, I'd like to put forth a few theses which would serve as an aide-memoire needed to prove the elements of the JCE. I believe we are all familiar with those elements, so I won't go into them, per se. An important characteristic of a JCE is that there is a criminal common purpose in existence. This common purpose can be twofold. The purpose of it can be to implement a goal arranged as part of a collective. That is why we have the term "common purpose." The second goal could be to achieve something which is not criminal in and by -- by and of itself, but that criminal goal is tempted by committing crimes. Therefore, we need to view both the means and goals. We also need to have an agreement among JCE members about these criminal means and goals. Having analysed the indictment, the opening statement of the OTP, and their final trial brief, we established that the Prosecution, in its final brief, explains the concept of JCE and significantly changes the concept of JCE in its first form. Secondly, we established that the Prosecution changed its thesis about the time of creation of the JCE, Form 2, as well as in terms of detention and persecution. This will be the subject of our analysis in the next one hour, approximately. Let us have a look at what is the goal of the alleged JCE, as put forth by the Prosecution, and what were the means to be used in order to establish or achieve the goal, as defined by the OTP. The goal or the objective of the alleged JCE are, inter alia, defined by the Prosecution in paragraph 5 of their final trial brief. I quote: [In English] "The objective of this JCE was to establish an autonomous Croat-dominated entity (the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna) on the territory of BiH that would at some point be linked to Croatia, whether by accession or another form of close association." [Interpretation] Therefore, the Prosecution state that the objective of the JCE was, first of all, to establish a Croatian entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina and, secondly, that there should be close links between that Croatian entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. We will address those objectives from the legal point of view, and I undertake full responsibility for the legal definitions offered. We will also address this matter from the point of view of Milivoj Petkovic and his understanding of the situation in 1992 and 1993. To start with, let's have a look at the case law of this Tribunal about the political goals of common purpose. The first-instance judgement in the Martic case, in paragraph 442, states as follows: [In English] "The evidence establishes the existence as of early 1991 of a political objective to unite Serb areas in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbia in order to establish an unified territory. Moreover, the evidence establishes that the SAO Krajina and subsequently Republika SRK government and authorities fully embrace and advocated this objective and strove to accomplish it in co-operation with the Serb leadership in Serbia and in Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Trial Chamber considers that such an objective, that is to unite with other ethnically similar areas, in and of itself does not amount to a common purpose within the meaning of the law on JCE pursuant to Article 1 of the Statute. However, where the creation of such authorities [sic] is intended to be implemented through the commission of crimes within the Statute, this may be sufficient to amount to a common criminal purpose." [Interpretation] The Appeals Chamber in the Martic case confirmed this position. Let us conclude, therefore, that this Tribunal ascertained that the political goals of unifying certain parts of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina with Croatia is not a criminal common plan. If the aforementioned goal is intended to be achieved by committing crimes, such a plan may suffice to believe that there is a JCE in existence. If we apply this rule to our proceedings, we conclude the following: The plan to establish a territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina that would be primarily populated by Croatia, with close ties to the Republic of Croatia, cannot be seen as a criminal common plan. My learned friend, Ms. Nozica, reminded us that the current topic in Bosnia-Herzegovina now is the establishment of a Croatian entity, and Mr. Scott confirmed that by having said that the US ambassador in Bosnia-Herzegovina is against such an initiative, which is beyond dispute, and it is also something that is very important for us is that such an initiative is on the table and that nobody even attempted to pronounce it a criminal concept. Let us see what see what Mr. Petkovic thought about that principle in 1992 and 1993. The first document, 4D2510, which is an excerpt from Mladic's diary for the 29th of November, 1992. Petkovic met Mladic in the presence of General Morillon, under the auspices of UNPROFOR, and Petkovic said this to Mladic and General Morillon, Let us try to come up with a solution by having the three sides sit down at the table in Bosnia-Herzegovina, let us stop to refer to Tudjman and Croatia all the time. The next document is even more important. It is P2019, the notes taken by Tihomir Blaskic during a meeting of the 21st of April, 1993. We saw it a number of times in this courtroom. Let's look at it again. Halilovic says: "Your top politicians advocate the establishment of the Croatian state on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Petkovic's response is this: "Well, you ought to be reasonable enough to know that Croatia cannot go for the annexation of B and H territory, because in that case it would lose its own territory." What Petkovic had in mind were the Serbs in the Republic of Croatia who also wanted to carve out a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina territory for themselves. Mr. Petkovic had the following to say about this document at page 49677 and 49678: [In English] "Let me first say what I replied to Halilovic. I said to him, You must be out of your mind if you really think that's the case. Croatia is an integral part of its territory, the Serbian Krajina which wishes to leave Croatia, and it is a crazy idea to think that Croatia, given this unsolved problem, aspires to anything more; something along those lines. So I'm not sure whether it was -- how faithfully it was recorded in that document. But, anyway, as far as I'm concerned, I was never in favour of the idea that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina should join Croatia. Instead, Bosnia and Herzegovina was a unified country and stayed this way, only I'm sorry that nowadays they can't seem to be able to run their own affairs." The conclusion is that Petkovic at the time believed that nobody in their right mind could seriously ponder an annexation of B and H territory with Croatia. For Petkovic, as a career military person, was the beginning and the end of the story of Greater Croatia. Hence, this Defence will not touch upon that topic any further. Let us look at what the Prosecutor has to say about the planned means used to achieve the objectives of the alleged JCE. In the indictment, in paragraph 15, the Prosecutor defines those means, and they say that all such means are planned simultaneously and, at the latest, as of the 18th of November, 1991. In the OTP final trial brief, they identified the alleged means of the JCE as follows: They defined what the original or core JCE 1 is. They state that it includes the crimes of persecution, deportation, and forcible transfer. Next, they define an expanded form of the JCE Form 1, which occurred in mid-1993, according to the Prosecution. Form 2, detention and deportation, is also taken into account. And according to the Prosecution, it came about on the 1st of July, 1993. In our belief, this amounts to a significant change of their definition of JCE 1. We believe that by having done this, the Prosecutor confirmed that the 30th of June, 1993, was a turning point in the relations of Croats and Muslims. Let us look at the following table. Here in this table, Your Honours, we wanted to show you, in a simple and easy-to-read manner, what the Prosecution state. In red, you will see the core JCE. These are -- these also include crimes against property, but they can also be found in the third form. It is obvious from this table that the Prosecution thinks that on 30 June 1993, in the area of Herceg-Bosna, something happened that represented a drastic change in the relations between the Muslim side and the Croatian side. If you allow me to draw some conclusions from that, I will put the following to you: There is no evidence that Petkovic ever made an agreement with anybody or joined any agreement, if such an agreement existed at all, that any political goal in Herceg-Bosna would be pursued by criminal means, by committing war crimes. The Petkovic Defence agrees with the Prosecution that 30 June 1993 was a turning point in the relations between the Croat and Muslim side in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We differ, however, when it comes to the reasons for that drastic change in their relations. The Prosecution's position is that in mid-1993, the authorities of the Herceg-Bosna simply decided to evolve the nature and scope of crimes in order to establish a Croat-dominated entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Petkovic Defence's position is the following: Herceg-Bosna was already established, up and running, as of April 1992. Secondly, the Herceg-Bosna authorities were not planning on widening or enlarging the territories under their control, which is corroborated by Petkovic's report for the period from 14 April through 31 December 1992. The document reference is P907. He says that in 1994, the Herceg-Bosna authorities had under their control 90 per cent of the territory planned as a territory of the HZ-HB, or the Croatian entity, with the corrections possible. Correction of the year. It's 1992. In April 1993, the BH Army launched offensive actions against the HVO, and until mid-1993, gained control over the entire Konjic municipality, except for two small enclaves, and they continued operations in two directions, Gornji Vakuf in the north and Mostar in the south; and in Central Bosnia they had taken Kakanj and Travnik. The fourth difference: On 30 June 1993, in co-operation with HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, the BH Army took control over the whole area north of East Mostar toward Jablanica. This was the alarm for taking special security measures. This, Your Honours, was the event that marked the turning point in the relations between Croats and Muslims in Herceg-Bosna. Everything that happened in Herceg-Bosna after 30 June 1993 was not the consequence of a criminal plan, but rather the consequence of security measures that were forced upon the authorities by the situation on the ground. Let me repeat. There is no evidence at all that anybody, on 30 June 1993, planned crimes against the Muslim population and the BH Army in order to achieve a political goal. Let us take a look at what was happening on the ground. The Prosecution witnesses mostly spoke about the Croats, that is, the HVO, as the party that caused the conflicts, as of April 1993. The Defence tried to show that it wasn't the case, but rather that the conflict started with the attacks of the BH Army and that they developed as these offensive activities gained momentum. There is an undisputed fact, though, that from April 1993, the BH Army enlarged the territory under its control. If we totally ignore the question who the first was, who started the conflict, because we cannot agree there, we will agree that the BH Army was in an offensive, that it was taking new territories, and that the areas marked green here are getting larger, whereas the areas marked blue, controlled by the HVO, are getting smaller. Let us look at map 4D561. This is a map for the period of March and April 1993. On this map, which we know well, you will see that at that moment, there were conflicts in and around Konjic and Gornji Vakuf and that the BH Army attacked HVO forces in and around Vitez, the attack coming from Zenica. If you look at the connection between Busovaca and Kiseljak, you will see that it is no longer possible to travel between these two towns. That's why I wish to remind you of a document that we analysed here in this courtroom, which is 4D392. This is a report of the Security Administration of the Supreme Command of the BH Army, dated 18 January 1993. The document says, I quote: "The Security Sector estimates that the BH Army forces in this area, in case of serious clashes, are able to fight back the HVO forces successfully, under the condition that the road communications between Busovaca, Kiseljak and Fojnica, as well as Busovaca, Vitez and Travnik, are cut." If we look at the sketch, then we'll see that the road between Busovaca and Kiseljak had already been cut, which happened in January 1993, and in April 1993, efforts are made to cut the road from Vitez to Travnik or Vitez -- from Vitez to Busovaca. The situation on the ground, therefore, is exactly what the Security Administration of the BH Army suggested in January 1993. Let us look at the following map, IC1183. We see the same area as before, but in June 1993. We see that the BH Army has full control over Kakanj and Travnik. Let's look at what happened in and around Mostar. The map is IC1184, the situation until 30 June 1993. We see here that the BH Army, marked green, has under its control East Mostar, and there is no direct communication with their own forces in the north and the south. But that wasn't much of a problem, because up until that time there was some sort of co-operation between the two armies in this area. Map IC1185, for the same period, shows a wider area. We see that in and around Jablanica and Konjic, the BH Army has full control, except over two small enclaves marked blue. One of them would disappear within a month. What is happening on the 30th of June, 1993? Let's take a look at map 4D622. The BH Army put all areas north and south of East Mostar under its control. Let's look at map IC1186. What does it look like if we take a wider view that also shows Jablanica and Konjic? East Mostar, after 30 June 1993, is directly linked with Jablanica, Konjic, and further on to Central Bosnia. We can draw the following conclusions: Firstly, the evidence clearly and unambiguously shows that the BH Army launched offensive military operations, as of April 1993, and continually widened the territory under its control. Secondly, the Petkovic Defence does not challenge the legality and legitimacy of the military actions of the BH Army because war, or combat activity by armed forces, unfortunately, are not an illegal means to achieve political objectives. Thirdly, the military activities of the BH Army are relevant in this case as evidence, as proof that certain measures taken by the Herceg-Bosna authorities were a reaction to and the consequence of the BH Army offensive, their actions and plans, rather than a criminal common plan agreed upon by the members of the alleged JCE. And thus, Your Honours, we are getting to the crucial date in this case, 30 June 1993, the date when the order to isolate and disarm the Muslim soldiers of the HVO was issued, the day when the order was issued to isolate conscripts of the BH Army. Let us look at these sketches once more. I'm referring to IC1184. Likewise, I refer to map 4D622, and we'll see what happened on the ground. Let me repeat once more the BH Army established control over the territories north and south of East Mostar so that East Mostar was linked with Central Bosnia. Let us take a look at the documents about that. The first document is 2D1389. This is a report of the staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces in Sarajevo about combat activities on 30 June 1993. What we see from this document is what the BH Army is. I'll repeat the document number, 2D1389. The document precisely lists what the BH Army took or had taken by 30 June 1993. It's not only the North Camp, as suggested by the Prosecution not only in the indictment, but also in all subsequent briefs, including the final brief. Apart from the North Camp, the following had been taken: Rastani, Vrapcici, Bijelo Polje, Salakovac, and Rosci. This report goes on to say, Your Honours, that the BH Army is holding all hydro power-plants on the Neretva River except for the Capljina plant. When you analyse the situation in Mostar, Your Honours, please take into consideration this document, which is one of the documents showing that the BH Army had control over the hydro power-plants on the Neretva River. And the third important part of this document is the final paragraph, which says that the forces of the 4th and the 6th Corps linked up in the areas around Mostar and Jablanica, and it says, I quote: "... which will have a positive effect on the coming combat operations." The following document we consider extremely important is 2D448. This is Arif Pasalic's speech on War Radio, given on June 30th, 1993 at 1100 hours [as interpreted], Your Honours, I stress 1100 hours [as interpreted]. Arif Pasalic said, I quote: "People, citizens of Mostar, you have to understand that this is judgement day, when you have to start fighting. I call on each citizen who can carry a rifle, who can carry a rock, to kill Ustasha criminals." This, Your Honours, was the start of all-out war in Mostar. The BH Army established control over areas north and south of East Mostar in co-operation with Muslim HVO soldiers. This, Your Honours, is the fact which makes these activities around Mostar different from all previous activities by the BH Army or any other activities. That's why the Muslim HVO soldiers, especially in and around Mostar, Stolac and Capljina, became a security issue. Let us remind ourselves of what the foreigners said about that. I will refer to three documents by foreign observers, the last two being under seal. I will only refer to them by number, but will refrain from mentioning the authors of the documents. And I warn against showing the documents outside the courtroom. I believe that this is sufficient protection, but if you think that we should go into private session, I'm not opposed to that. The first document is P3952. This is a report by the European Monitors, dated 4 August 1993. It says in the report, I quote: [In English] "Also, since about five weeks, the HVO has decided a large-scale arrest operation of all the Muslim male between 16 and 60 in all the territory under their control. These operations have followed the mutiny of Muslim soldiers of the HVO, who have given the opportunity to B and --" I never can pronounce that in English, "Bosnia-Herzegovina Army to create a horseback corridor between Jablanica and Mostar along the Neretva River." [Interpretation] The following document, which is under seal so it should not be broadcast outside the courtroom, is P4698A. In this document, it says, among others, I quote: [In English] "It seems that the operation was triggered off during the night of June 29/30th, when the Muslims enlisted in the HVO 3rd Brigade with the base in the Tihomir Misic Barracks deserted their weapons to join the ranks of the BiH. Seizing this opportunity, the Muslims advanced north and reached Bijelo Polje." [Interpretation] The following document is P2979. It is also under seal. It should not be broadcast outside the courtroom. Under item 3, it says, among others, that HVO forces are concerned because Muslims are leaving the 3rd Brigade and joining the forces of the BH Army. Now, Your Honours, we wish to show you documents that show that Muslim HVO soldiers, under such circumstances, really became a security problem, and that it was justified from the security point of view to take some measures. The first document is 4D1461. This is a SIS document issued in September 1992, and it says, amongst other things, and I quote: "Muharem Dizdar, one of the HVO commanders, and Ragib Dizdar, visited Muslim members of the HVO, and they told them not to leave the HVO units, or rather not to join the BiH Army until the hour was right, and that they would inform them when that happened." The following document is 4D469, an official record originating from the Crime Department, where it says: "Pressures put on the Muslims who are members of the HVO and the MUP units to leave those units, if they didn't do so, they were threatened to be killed or their house to be set on fire. The following document, 4D568, issued by the Security Administration of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the author is Fikret Muslimovic, and it says here, I quote: "It is realistic to [indiscernible] further tensions in relations and even an all-out military confrontation between the RBiH army and the HVO. It is very important to prepare ourselves for such situation and to inactivate the Muslims who are in the HVO and to exercise influence on them to move over from the HVO to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." The following document is 4D33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Alaburic. I only would like to ask the interpreters that in the English booth, there is so much voice -- or, sorry, not voice only, but noise that it is impossible to listen to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that our colleagues in the booth will appreciate and will act accordingly. Let's look at 4D33. This is an assessment of the security situation. It was issued by the security organ of the 42nd Mountain Brigade, which says, amongst other things, and I quote: "Call upon all Muslim members of the HVO to place themselves on the side of their people." The following document is 4D34. The same author, only two days later on the 18th of April, 1993, he proposes as follows, and I quote: "... to establish co-operation with our soldiers in the HVO and point out the seriousness of the situation to them." The following document, 4D35, the commander of the 42nd Mountain Brigade, Bajro Pizovic, says, amongst other things, a plan for forming of Muslim soldiers in HVO units in Mostar, Capljina and Stolac has to be prepared. The following document is 4D00473. The same author, Bajro Pizovic, on the 18th of April, wrote to the commander of the 1st Brigade of the HVO, Nedjeljko Obradovic, and says, and I quote: "I mention, and this is well known to you, that a large number of Muslim soldiers are in your units, and they are all Muslims, and they belong to this people, so it wouldn't be good if a defined organisation and formation of your units was disrupted." Your Honours, I would like to remind you that our witness, Mr. Bozo Pavlovic, who was an officer in the 1st Brigade, interpreted this document as a direct threat, and that's exactly how the HVO understood it at the time. The following document is 4D36. This document was issued by Arif Pasalic on the 2nd of May, 1993. It is a report about the situation in the territory of the 42nd Mountain Brigade that was around Stolac and Capljina. We would like to point out three parts, where it says: "Linking up with our men in the HVO was carried out." It says also: "Men from the Capljina HVO have the task of taking Tasovcici village ..." And, thirdly: "Villages have maximum security," or, rather: "Seize the town of Stolac with our people in the HVO." That's the end of quote. This points directly to a link between the BiH Army and Muslims in the HVO. We would also like to highlight the testimony of a protected witness, Witness CR. Can we somehow make sure that the image is not broadcast. On transcript page 11858 and 11859, Witness CR said that during the first three months of 1993, the Muslim authorities advised Muslims to leave the HVO police. Based on all of the above, I would like to conclude the following: Firstly, if the HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity joined the ABiH in other parts of the South-East Herzegovina Operation Zone, the authorities of Herceg-Bosna could easily lose control over the territory of entire Mostar, Stolac and Capljina municipalities. Secondly, ABiH Army documents establish beyond any doubt that the ABiH prepared military actions in co-operation with certain members of the HVO Muslim soldiers. Thirdly, immediate security measures had to be taken under such circumstances. Let's remind everybody that Muslim soldiers accounted for a large percentage of HVO units. In Mostar, it was 50 per cent. HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity were disarmed and interned. What we wanted to demonstrate as part of our Defence is this: Croatians did not rejoice -- rejoice at disarming their Muslim colleagues. That measure was a necessary security measures aimed at preventing the loss of control in the territory stretching from Mostar to the Adriatic coast. The order on disarmament and isolation was issued on the same day, on the 30th of June, 1993, and the order was issued to Milivoj Petkovic by the supreme commander, Mate Boban. And Petkovic, in his turn, issued the same order to his subordinate, the head of the operations zone, Mr. Miljenko Lasic. Petkovic does not say that he did not issue the order, and as we go on we will try to show you that it was legal and that it was militarily justified. In other words, Petkovic participated in the implementation of the decision, thinking that he was acting legally and justly. On the 30th of June, 1993, Petkovic testified that that was the most difficult day in his life, and that was confirmed by our witness, Bozo Pavlovic, who personally took part in the disarmament of his own Muslim soldiers. Your Honours, we wanted to show you that the isolation of Muslim soldiers of the HVO was a justified security measure and that, before the 30th of June, 1993, Muslims enjoyed the same rights in the HVO as Croats. Military commanders protected their own Muslim soldiers when certain security services pointed to possible security issues due to a large share of Muslims in HVO units in the territory of Mostar, Capljina and Stolac. Muslim soldiers remained HVO soldiers even after isolation. The period of their incarceration in a detention centre is considered time served in the HVO. That's how things were, and that's how things should be. Your Honours, I believe we have reached the time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. I was signalling to you just a minute ago to tell you that. Yes, it's the time for our first 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We continue, and, Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I promised our colleagues in the French booth that I will slow down in the rest of my argument. I apologise to them for not having borne in mind the fact that they are interpreting with a bit of a delay and I was too fast. Your Honours, in our presentation, in our final argument, in our closing brief, we have reached the topic of imprisonments which started on the 30th of June, 1993. In his final brief, in paragraph 313, the Prosecutor speaks about that, and as we go on, we will analyse that paragraph sentence by sentence. In the first sentence, the Prosecutor claims that pursuant to Petkovic's order dated 30 June 1993, the Muslim able-bodied men were all imprisoned. Let's focus on the words "all Muslim able-bodied men," which implies all conscripts in Herceg-Bosna. Let's look at Petkovic's order, P03019. We have seen it dozens of times in this courtroom, but let's look at it once again. Petkovic issued his order and sent it only to one operation zone, not to all four operations zones, but to just one operation zone, the South-East Herzegovina Operation Zone. The estimate was that the security issue existed primarily in that zone. And let's look at the document, where it says that the OZ commander sent this order to the 2nd and 3rd Brigades, but not to the 1st Brigade. Furthermore, Petkovic ordered that Muslim soldiers of the HVO and conscripts of the BH Army who were on the reserve strength of the ABiH forces to be isolated. We will talk about that further on. It arises from this order that civilians had to be left in their homes. This order, issued by Milivoj Petkovic, was lawful, and no crime could be committed through the execution of that order, and we will provide a lengthy explanation of that as we go on. The next sentence in paragraph 313 -- or, rather, the next two sentences contain an allegation that civilians were also arrested. In footnote 714, the Prosecutor refers to a number of documents which we analysed very thoroughly, and we were able to establish that a majority of those documents, or at least one part of those documents, refers to the month of May 1993. In other words, a lot of those documents had nothing whatsoever to do with this isolation measure which was carried out starting on the 1st of July, 1993. The analysis of the remainder of the document shows that in this footnote, the Prosecutor fails to mention a single piece of evidence that would confirm his argument about the incarceration of civilians. And the following sentence reads and contains an allegation about the detention of women, children and elderly. The footnote number is 715. An analysis of this footnote also shows that there is no proof about the incarceration of civilians. I would especially like to draw your attention to two documents. One of them is P3133. This is a report dated the 3rd of July, which was compiled by the Department for Crime Prevention. In this report, it says that a list of persons under 18 and over 60 years of age has been compiled, and they have to be let go. In other words, people of a younger age and people of an older age were not supposed to be arrested in the first place on the 1st of July, 1993, or later on. Now let's also look at P4822, which is Mazowiecki's report dated September 1993, where it says that militarily able-bodied males were arrested, but there were also examples where people younger and older were also isolated. We conclude that on the 30th of June, 1993, and later on, no civilians were incarcerated. And, Your Honours, now we come to an issue that General Petkovic's Defence regards the key issue in these proceedings. For us, the topic of a Greater Croatia or a Croatian entity are not crucial topics in these proceedings. For us, the crucial topic concerns the categories of detained persons. What was the status of a people detained in the detention centres of Herceg-Bosna? The Prosecutor, in paragraph 142 of their final brief, state the following categories: First of all, Muslim soldiers of the HVO; secondly, POWs; and, three, civilians. Your Honours, Petkovic's Defence completely agrees with the structure of these three categories, but this is where our agreement ends. First, a few words about Muslim HVO soldiers. In their final brief, the OTP, in paragraphs 144 to 149, say that the Muslim HVO soldiers were neither civilians, nor POWs. The Petkovic Defence agrees. Further on, the Prosecution states that the Muslim soldiers were persons protected by Article 75 of the Additional Protocol 1 and Common Article 3, as people "hors de combat" due to their detention. Concerning this international law of protection of Muslim HVO soldiers, the Petkovic Defence disagrees, and I will explain why. I believe everyone in this courtroom will agree that in order to interpret a legal norm, it is essential to establish where it is in the legal body. If it is in the part concerning civilians, it is deemed relevant to civilians. If it is found in the parts concerning POWs, then it has to do with POWs. Article 75 of the Additional Protocol 1 is in the civilian population part, in section 3, Chapter 1: [In English] "Field of application and protection of persons and objects." [Interpretation] The first article of that chapter is Article 72, defining field of application, and it clearly states that the entire part of that protocol has to do with civilians. Based on that, Your Honours, we conclude that Article 75 of Additional Protocol 1 does not concern own soldiers. Let us look at whether Common Article 3 could concern Muslim HVO soldiers. Persons "hors de combat" due to detention are defined by Article 41 of AP 1. Inter alia, it is stated that a person is "hors de combat" if held by the enemy. Based on that, Your Honours, we conclude that the Muslim HVO soldiers were not in the power of an adverse party. They were and remain HVO soldiers. The time spent in detention is counted towards their service; their service with the HVO, that is, and we have shown examples of that. Muslim HVO soldiers, therefore, were not "hors de combat," and Common Article 3 does not apply. We conclude, therefore, that Muslim HVO soldiers were protected by national law. If a crime was committed against them, it is a matter of domestic and not international law. And an important legal rule to mention is this: In case of ambiguity or legal uncertainty on that point, the interpretation of the law the most favourable to the accused must prevail. In their final briefs, the Valentin Coric and General Petkovic's Defence addressed the issue of the status of Muslim HVO soldiers, and you could also refer to the relevant parts of our final brief. This brings us, Your Honour, to what we believe is the crux or the core of this case, which is the military able-bodied men or military conscripts in Bosnia and Herzegovina and their status in case of detention. The Prosecutor believed that those persons were civilians. We, on the other hand, consider them to be POWs. Why is this question important at all? Namely, we do not dispute that POWs and civilians, once detained, need to be treated humanely. There is no dispute in that. However, the definition of their status is essential for the following reasons, which we marked in red in our presentation. It is important because the crimes of imprisonment of Article 2 and 5 of the Statute cannot be committed against POWs. It is important because the crime of deportation of civilians cannot be committed against POWs. It is important because the crime of forcible transfer cannot be committed against POWs. It is important because the crime of persecution cannot be committed against POWs, with one remark. The Petkovic Defence is, of course, familiar with the fact that POWs can be victims of crimes against humanity, but in such a case it has to be a part of a widespread and/or systematic attack against a civilian population. To put it shortly, if the able-bodied men of Bosnia-Herzegovina were POWs and not civilians, then there is no core JCE 1, or at least that JCE 1 is substantially different than pleaded by the Prosecution. Let's have a look at the status of able-bodied men as defined by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and its case law and what it has to do -- what it has to say about the relevance of mens rea in order to perform certain actions against POWs. We believe it most appropriate, Your Honours, to point out the position of the Appeals Chamber in the Kordic case and what they had to say about the status of able-bodied men. Many paragraphs are relevant. However, we believe that it suffices for us to point out paragraph 608 and 615 of the appeals judgement. You have the relevant portions on the screens. I will merely sum up the position of the Appeals Chamber. First of all, able-bodied men are not considered civilians unless proven otherwise. The second rule of thumb is that children, women and elderly are considered civilians until proven otherwise. Hence, therefore, for the able-bodied men, a different presumption stands, as opposed to the children, women and the elderly. The Petkovic Defence believes that position to be appropriate. In these proceedings, the Prosecutor was supposed to prove the civilian status of able-bodied men, because an able-bodied man is considered a civilian if his status as civilian is proven by the Prosecutor beyond any reasonable doubt. Pending that, able-bodied men are not considered civilians. The case law of this Tribunal mentions the relevance of the mens rea. We believe the most appropriate example would be the appeals judgement in the Mrksic case, paragraph 42. In the final part, it states, I quote: [In English] "... the Trial Chamber's finding, unchallenged by the parties, that the perpetrators of the crimes in Ovcara acted in the understanding that their acts were directed against members of the Croatian armed forces. The fact that they acted in such a way precludes that they intended that their acts form part of the attack against the civilian population of Vukovar ..." [Interpretation] In other words, it is crucial to determine whether certain activities were undertaken with the necessary mens rea and the wish to treat members of the opposing force in a particular way. Evidence shows that the authorities of Herceg-Bosna considered able-bodied men the reserve force of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was the position of the Petkovic Defence, and we expanded on it in our final brief, among others, in paragraph 279. For a start, let us have a look at what International Humanitarian Law has to say on the point of reservists. We believe it to be the most appropriate to indicate a portion from a book called "Customary International Humanitarian Law" by Henckaerts and Doswald-Beck. I wanted to quote two paragraphs towards the end of the book. I quote: "While in some countries entire segments of the population between certain ages may be drafted into the armed forces in the event of armed conflict, only those persons who are actually drafted, that is, who are actually incorporated into the armed forces, can be considered combatants. Potential mobilisation does not render the person concerned a combatant liable to attack. "Footnote: This conclusion is based on discussions during the second consultation with academic and governmental experts in the framework of this study in May 1999 and the general agreement among the experts to this conflict. The experts also considered that it may be necessary to consider the legislation of a state in determining when reservists actually become members of the armed forces." [Interpretation] End of quote. I wish to put forth the position on the Petkovic Defence. Firstly, members of armed forces can be combatants and non-combatants. Combatants are those taking direct part in combat. Non-combatants are those taking part in various so-called non-combat services in the armed forces. Secondly, if captured, both have the status of POWs. Thirdly, military conscripts who are not mobilised are not combatants. Fourthly, military conscripts who are not mobilised could be members of the armed forces, but then they are non-combatants. Fifthly, in order to establish whether in Bosnia and Herzegovina military conscripts were members of the armed forces, one needs to study the legislation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let's have a look at that particular legislation. The first document is 4D412, Decree Law on Service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Article 7: "The army shall be composed of the standing and reserve forces." Article 9 of the decree law states as follows, I quote: "The reserve force of the army shall comprise persons who are, according to the provisions regulating conscription, subject to service in the reserve force of the army." The next document is Decree Law on Compulsory Military Service, number 4D1030. In Article 4, it is stated that compulsory military service shall consist of the recruitment obligation. And Article 7 states that compulsory military service shall cease for men at the end of the calendar year in which the age of 60 is reached. Let us conclude, then, Your Honours. According to B and H legislation, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina comprised active and reserve forces. Secondly, able-bodied men of a certain age, that is to say, military conscripts, were members of the reserve forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thirdly, military conscripts were not combatants, but they were non-combatant members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of the reserve forces. Let us look at a number of documents to see whether the legislation was, indeed, implemented in such a way in the field. We will first look at the documents of the Muslim side. Let us start with 4D430. It is from mid-April 1993. It is a combat report which states as follows: "Civilians from the village of Doljani are being evacuated at the moment. Conscripts will remain." This document clearly confirms that military conscripts are not civilians, as viewed by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The next document is 1D349. It is a document drafted by the Jablanica Municipal Assembly War Presidency on 9 May 1993. Among other things, it states that mobilisation should be carried out of all able-bodied population between the age of 15 and 65 in order to man work units, military units, civilian protection units, and other units formed in the municipality of Jablanica. Therefore, military able-bodied men of a certain age did have certain obligations. The next document, 1D1410, is a decision of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It regulates the status of citizens, which, among other things, states that military conscripts can receive permission to depart for a third country only if they are ill. Those who are not must return to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Assembly points will be set up for them under the auspices of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: This document was a government decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is P9208 by Mr. Zecic, who said, and I quote, that "only able-bodied men remained in the village." The testimony of Witness Husnija Mahmutovic on transcript page 25694. The witness confirmed that all healthy men of military age were obliged to join the BH Army. The following document is P9198. It's the statement of Witness Zahirovic, who, speaking about himself and his colleagues, once says "people fit for military service," and on another occasion, "members of the BH Army," by which he unambiguously places a sign of equation between persons fit for military service and members of the BH Army. And the following document is from a protected witness and should not be broadcast outside the courtroom. The document number is P10220. Witness U said, I quote. "Of course, when I was released from Heliodrom, just like any other military conscript, I reported to the closest military unit." [Interpretation] We conclude, Your Honours, that these, as many other documents of the BH Army, confirm that the practice was in line with the laws and regulations. Conscripts were considered members of the BH Army. We said, in the introductory part, that it's equally important how the BH authorities perceived military able-bodied men and military conscripts, so let us look at some testimonies. Milivoj Petkovic, transcript page 49579. He testified about how he considered -- able-bodied Muslim men were considered by him to be members of the BH Army. Witness Zrinko Tokic considered conscripts soldiers, as noted on transcript page 45373 and the following. Witness Filipovic spoke extensively about that. I will quote Judge Antonetti, who summarised Filipovic's extensive testimony: [In English] "As I understand it, in your view there were no civilians, as a smatter of fact, apart from women and children. Any man, maybe except very old men, any man could be a soldier; is that right? "That's correct." [Interpretation] That was the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at some official minutes, and we'll see what the Government of Herceg-Bosna -- what their position was of the status of men who are conscripts. The document is P4841. These are minutes from the working meeting held on 6 September 1993. It is clearly stated that the persons taken prisoner were members of the standing -- standing personnel of the BH Army or members of the reserve; that is, active-duty or reserve members. I could quote other documents, but there is no doubt about the position of the authorities that members of the reserve were considered members of the BH Army. I'm now going to summarise all this in 12 points. Firstly, the crime of imprisonment under Article 5(E) of the Statute and the crime of unlawful confinement of civilian under Article 2(G) of the Statute can be committed only and exclusively in relation to civilians. Secondly, crimes of imprisonment, unlawful confinement, cannot be committed by the internment of prisoners of war. Thirdly, military-able men were not civilians until proved otherwise. Fourthly, Muslim HVO soldiers were not protected persons by international law. They were protected by national laws, and that is why this Tribunal is not competent to decide about crimes committed against one's own soldiers, irrespective of their ethnic affiliation. Five, by internment of Muslim HVO soldiers and military-able men of Muslim ethnicity who had the status of prisoners of war, crimes of imprisonment, unlawful confinement, of civilians could not be committed. Six, sub-item 1. On the 30th of June, 1993, Milivoj Petkovic, upon the order of the supreme commander, issued an order that Muslim HVO soldiers in the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone be disarmed and isolated and that military-able Muslim men shall also be isolated. Sub-item 2. The order was lawful and justified by security considerations. Sub-item 3, civilians were supposed to be protected. And here we can see once more an excerpt from Petkovic's order, which is document P3019. Seventh conclusion. Civilians were not supposed to be detained upon Petkovic's order. If a civilian was arrested, after all, he or she had to be released immediately. Eighth conclusion. Disarmament and isolation of Muslim HVO soldiers and soldiers of the BH Army, both active and reserve, were not an attack directed against the civilian population. Nine, the disarmament and isolation of Muslims was not a discriminatory measure, as was explained by the Appeals Chamber in the Kordic case. I quote: [In English] "The Appeals Chamber considers that the detaining power must, within a reasonable time, process and decide whether detained persons are civilians. In the circumstances, the evidence does not support that the HVO carried out blanket detentions of all Muslim civilians, but rather suggests that men of military age between 18 and 60 were targeted." [Interpretation] The 10th conclusion is that the crime of persecution was not committed by internment of Muslim HVO soldiers and military-age men of Muslim ethnicity because the victims of the internment were not civilians and, therefore, the underlying act was not a crime. Moreover, that internment was not part of an attack against any civilian population. Conclusion 11. In accordance with the Geneva Convention number 3, Article 12, paragraph 2, prisoners of war may be transferred to a third country which is a party to the Convention. The transfer of prisoners of war is not a crime of unlawful deportation or transfer of civilians. And now a digression, with your leave. The Petkovic Defence, Your Honours, did not go into the issue of the transit centre in Ljubuski which was to be founded in July 1993 because it wasn't directly relevant for General Petkovic. And in our final brief, we couldn't afford to go into matters that are not directly essential for General Petkovic, so I will explain our position now. Since military-able men of Muslim ethnicity were considered the reserve army of the BH Army and, hence, they were prisoners of war, the initiative to establish a transit centre at Ljubuski was absolutely lawful and in line -- in keeping with the 3rd Geneva Convention, Article 12, paragraph 2. I remind you that the Herceg-Bosna authorities contacted the UNHCR and UNPROFOR for help in the establishment of their transit centre and the temporary transfer of prisoners of war to third countries. The UNHCR, upon consultation with their headquarters, concluded that they would thus contribute to ethnic cleansing, and refused to provide assistance, after which UNPROFOR pulled out as well. I think that these are facts for which there is ample evidence in the case file, which will be very important when you decide about the importance of this initiative, so I believe, Your Honours, that you will take this into consideration when you draw your conclusions on all the consequences of the situation in the detention centres. 11th conclusion. The JCE 1, as pleaded by the Prosecution, did not exist.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It is conclusion 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether or not a JCE 2, with regard to the conditions and confinement, actually existed is another matter which we will deal in the continuation of our closing arguments. Your Honours, I'm going to speak about the so-called Mrksic duty. We will state very openly, as has been our habit in the past five years, what, in our opinion, is the crucial thesis of these proceedings, such as determining which stone in a bridge determines its firmness and stability. We said that it's a status of the detained conscripts of the BH Army or, in other words, the question whether they are prisoners of war or civilians. The second most important question, to our minds, is about the responsibility for a failure to act; that is, the admission of liability, which is Article 7, paragraph 3 of the Statute, and which is also important for the question of responsibility under paragraph 7 -- Article 7, paragraph 1 of the Statute, which is about responsibility by commission or by omission. The duties prescribed by law or the legal duty to act we consider -- is something that we, the Petkovic Defence, consider very important. The Mrksic duty, what does the Prosecution say about that? To begin with, let us take a look at the context of the Mrksic case. We considered it most appropriate to show paragraph 1 from the first-instance judgement, in which there is a brief description of the context. I'll summarise it in one sentence. The Yugoslav People's Army handed over at least 264 detainees to Serb paramilitary units. The detainees were persons from the Vukovar Hospital. So the essence of this case is that the Yugoslav People's Army handed over detainees to Serb paramilitary units. The duty of military commanders, or the so-called Mrksic duty as determined in this case, does not exist if a military commander transfers prisoners of war to the military police of their own armed forces, their own civilian police, official prisons or detention facilities. The reason for that is very simple, and I think it most appropriate to give an example, an example from your life. The military commander of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade from the area around Konjic and Jablanica, in April 1993, transferred some 80-odd soldiers of the BH Army taken prisoner in Sovici to the Ljubuski Prison. That military commander stays in his area, that is, around Konjic and Jablanica, has no contact whatsoever with the Ljubuski Prison, and has no authority over it. Therefore, he cannot be responsible for the treatment of prisoners of war in that prison, and that includes the prisoners of war he, himself, transferred to that prison. Accordingly, the military commander's duty with regard to prisoners of war ceases at the moment when he hands them over to the military police, the police, or the detention centre over which that military commander has no de jure or de facto authority, just as testified to by General Praljak, General Petkovic and other witnesses. Let us see what the Prosecution says about that in their final brief in paragraphs 140 and 302. They refer to the Mrksic case and the Appeals Chamber judgement, and more specifically paragraph 273.
