Briefly, the Prosecution considers all prisoners in this case agents of the detaining power and, therefore, they had a duty to protect the prisoners. Let us look at the entire paragraph 73 from the Mrksic appeals judgement. We will see that the duty to protect prisoners of war concerns those who have custody of prisoners, and that's why an agent, in the sense of the Mrksic duty, is not every military commander, or every official in Herceg-Bosna, or any other territorial jurisdiction. An agent is only one -- or only those into whose custody prisoners of war have come into. Let me conclude. The legal duty as identified by the Appeals Chamber in the Mrksic case only applies to those agents of the detaining power who find themselves with custody of prisoners of war, that is, not any and every agent of that state, but only those who had that responsibility as they were effectively custodians of the prisoners of war. Second conclusion, international law does not regulate the issue of competence; it is left to each individual country to decide who is responsible to deal with prisoners of war. Thirdly, the Prosecution did not plead in these proceedings that any legislative enactment and/or superior order delegated the duty to protect detainees in any detention facility to the chief of the Main Staff. Number 4, there is no evidence that any legislative enactment and/or superior order delegated the duty to protect detainees in any detention facility to Milivoj Petkovic. Number 5, there is no evidence that the chief of the Main Staff, Petkovic, exercised control over any detention facility. Number 6, Prosecution did not plead that Petkovic found himself with the de facto custody over prisoners of war and/or other detainees. Number 7, there is no evidence that Petkovic had de facto custody over prisoners of war. And, finally, number 8, in conclusion, Mrksic's duty, even if it could be applied in this case, certainly does not apply to Milivoj Petkovic. The following topic regarding omissions, as explained by the Prosecution, is the so-called Celebici duty to release prisoners. The Prosecutor speaks about that in paragraph 308 of their final brief, and it is said there, amongst other things, and I quote: [In English] "By August 1993, all of the accused knew that they had imprisoned thousands of civilian detainees ..." [Interpretation] I'm skipping one part: [In English] "All of the accused, therefore, had a duty to release prisoners." [Interpretation] I would just like to say that in August 1993, Petkovic was the deputy commander, and he had the right to decide to an extent to which his commander or the joint [indiscernible] authorised him to do so. However, what matters here is this: Duty to release prisoners according to the international humanitarian law applies exclusively to civilians and not to prisoners of war. Let's look at Rule 128, Customary International Humanitarian Law. It's very clear. There's no obligation to release prisoners of war before the end of the conflict. The International Humanitarian Law does not prescribe obligations pertaining to one's own soldiers, and also the duty to release applies only to civilians. Based on that, we can conclude this armed and interned Muslim HVO soldiers were not civilians. Military-able men or military conscripts of the BiH Army were not civilians, but rather prisoners of war. The Herceg-Bosna authorities were not obliged to release Muslim HVO soldiers and military-able men from their detention centres. Your Honours, as I've already told you, we will not deal with detention centres. We will touch upon the conditions in detention centres, but we will be dealing with the prisoners' forced labour. And now as I continue presenting my closing argument, Your Honours, I would like to refer to the Prosecutor's argument about commanding generals or occupation commanders, and that term applies directly both to General Petkovic and General Praljak. In his final brief, the Prosecutor speaks about that in paragraphs 154, 155, 156 and 324. There are some other paragraphs that touch upon the topic. In a nutshell, Generals Petkovic and Praljak, according to the Prosecutor, shall be held responsible for aiding and abetting crimes committed against civilians at the time when they were heads of the Main Staff, for a simple reason: They were commanding generals at the time. Your Honours, we would like to draw your attention to the following facts. This is the first mention of occupying commanders, commanding generals, in these proceedings. No such thing was ever pleaded in the indictment. No such thing was ever mentioned or explained in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. This argument was never part of the Prosecution's opening statement. This argument was never part of the Prosecution case. The Prosecution did not lead any evidence to that effect. The thesis about Petkovic and Praljak as occupying generals is belated, and that's why it should be totally ignored by the Trial Chamber, it should be totally disregarded. However, we will be dealing with the Prosecutor's allegations, and we will try to demonstrate to you that contrary to the Prosecutor's allegation, the alleged obligation for protecting civilians in the occupying area was not, in general terms, part of the commanding general's duties. A special obligation to protect civilians in an occupied area concerned commanders of the occupation army who is assigned or appointed to govern an occupied territory. First of all, let's deal with the issue of whether Herceg-Bosna could ever be considered an occupied territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. To constitute an occupation as a matter of International Law, the occupation must be done by foreign forces. This arises clearly from the 1907 Hague Convention. This is beyond challenge in the legal theory, and here we have presented an excerpt from the book "The International Law of Belligerent Occupation" by Dinstein, and based on that we can conclude: Since an occupier has to be a foreign force, the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot be occupiers in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Secondly, Herceg-Bosna cannot be an occupying power in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There's no dispute about the fact that there's a difference between an international armed conflict, on the one hand, and occupation, on the other. My learned friend Mr. Bozo Kovacic said a few words about that, but I will also say a few words about that. Firstly, every occupation is, beyond any doubt, an international armed conflict. However, an international armed conflict does not have to be occupation. The difference between occupation and an international armed conflict arises from the level of control. For an international armed conflict, there has to be the so-called overall control over the territory of a different state, whether for an occupation to be in place, there has to be effective control over the territory of another state. Occupation is the question of fact, and the Prosecution has to prove the fact of occupation beyond any reasonable doubt. What I've just stated is very clear in legal theory, and I'm offering another excerpt from the book, "The International Law of Belligerent Occupation" and as well as from the book, "The International Law of Occupation." And here we also have an excerpt from the first-instance judgement in Naletilic judgement, paragraph 214. I believe that my learned friend Mr. Kovacic has already quoted that part, and I will repeat: [In English] "The overall control test submitted in the Blaskic trial judgement is not applicable to the determination of the existence of an occupation. The Chamber is of the view that there is an essential distinction between the determination of a state of occupation and that of the existence of an international armed conflict. The application of the overall control test is applicable to the latter. A further degree of control is required to establish occupation." [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to draw your attention to the fact that the Prosecution did not plead that Croatia occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let's look at the indictment, first of all, paragraph 232, where it says -- or, rather, this is the only paragraph where the term "occupation" is mentioned at all. We have prepared an excerpt from the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, paragraphs 232 -- there are many of them. However, everything boils down to the following. The Prosecutor is trying to demonstrate there was an overall control, that Croatia was directly involved, that it participated or intervened directly, the participation of the Croatian Army. However, there's no single word about occupation or effective control. Let's look at the adjudicated facts. We have tried to single out the most representative facts. Among the adjudicated facts, we can find those that lead to the conclusion that the Republic of Croatia took part in the organisation, planning and co-ordination of military operations; that Croatian Army units were involved in the conflict in the territory of Mostar. It was also established that Croatian Army units were present in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and that Croatian financed and provided military equipment to the HVO; that Croatia was thus involved in the control of the HVO forces, that Croatia exercised indirect control; that Croatia also provided manpower and lent substantial material assistance to the HVO. Again, Your Honours, look at the adjudicated facts, and you will see that there is no mention of occupation, there is no single word about effective control. Let's look at what the Prosecutor says in his final brief. In paragraphs 71 through 79, the Prosecutor speaks about an international armed conflict. There is a chapter where it says that Croatia had overall control, and then at Chapter 5 again there's a reference to Croatia's overall control, and another chapter where it says that the Croatian Army was extensively engaged in BiH. Therefore, save for the parts which might refer to Generals Praljak and Petkovic, the Prosecutor did not establish in his final brief that Croatia was an occupying force in Bosnia and Herzegovina or that it had effective control and, I repeat, effective control over the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let's conclude. Firstly, there is no documentary evidence that Croatia ever occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina. Secondly, there is no testimony or witness statement that Croatia occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am emphasising the word "occupy" or "the occupying force." Thirdly, there is no evidence that the Croatian Government had effective control in Herceg-Bosna. Four, the Prosecution has tried over the past five years that Croatia did have overall control, that Croatia gave substantial support to the authorities in the HVO armed forces, and that the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH, therefore, was not a civil war, but an international armed conflict. All allegations would be unnecessary if the Republic of Croatia had been an occupying force in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And now, number 5: The Prosecution neither pleaded nor proved that Croatia and the Croatian Army occupied part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thus, the Prosecution's submissions about occupation presented at the very end of the proceedings should be totally disregarded. We would now like to put something else within the context, and those are the contradictory statements on the part of the Prosecution about occupation and an armed conflict co-existing on the same territory at the same time. First of all, let's present the following thesis: Armed conflict or occupation are two alternatives. They cannot co-exist. You can have -- you cannot have at the same time, in the same place, an armed conflict, and then charge individuals pursuant to Articles 2, 4 and 5 of the Statute, and allege that at the same time, in the same place, there was also the state of occupation, which requires a much higher degree of concern for the civilians who reside in such an occupied territory. Let's look at an excerpt from the Geneva Convention 4, only a few articles where the staple formulation is "conflict" or "occupation." There are even parts of the Convention which regulate situations that exist during an armed conflict, and a special chapter which regulates the situation on an occupied territory. It is beyond every doubt that certain crimes may be committed only in an occupied territory, and they cannot be committed during an armed conflict. We would like to point out a comment from the Additional Protocol 1, Commentary 1700, and I will quote from the relevant portion of that commentary: [In English] "Any part of territory in which the occupant has been deprived of actual means for carrying out normal administration by the presence of opposing military forces would not have the status of occupied territory within the terms of Articles 2 and 42 of The Hague Regulations." [Interpretation] End of quote. The jurisprudence of the case law of this Tribunal is incomplete. Accord with that, I'm quoting from the first-sentence judgement from Naletilic, paragraph 217: [In English]"... battle areas may not be considered as occupied territory." [Interpretation] Based on that, Your Honours, we conclude that the state of armed conflict, on the one hand, and the state of occupation, on the other, cannot co-exist on the same territory, at the same time. The Prosecutor, however, claims that the contrary is possible, and then let's look at the situation that that may lead to. The Prosecution claims in the indictment and tried to lead evidence that major conflict between ABiH and the HVO was avoided until April 1993, and that from then until April 1994, there was continued fighting in Mostar and other areas. You can find this in paragraph 32, 111, 232 and 234 of the indictment. I will repeat the paragraph numbers. 32, 111, 232 and 234. Pursuant to this assertion, that there were continuing conflicts in the area, the Prosecution submitted a number of allegations for your assessment based on Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute, the acts which can be committed only during an armed conflict. That is why the Prosecution's assertion about continued fighting contradicts their assertions on the simultaneous state of occupation. We'd like to turn your attention to some evidence which clearly establishes the state of armed conflict from April onwards. There were conflicts in the area of Konjic and Jablanica as of April onwards, Central Bosnia from April on, Prozor from April onwards, Mostar from May, with a short interim period until the 30th of June, and onwards. In June 1993, Travnik fell in Central Bosnia. In June, Kakanj fell. Yes, I believe it was June, I believe. I must check that over the break. On the 30th of June, 1993, as we have already mentioned, the ABiH takes the territory to the east and south of Mostar. In July, they take control of the area towards Buna. In July 1993, the AB and H take control of Fojnica. In the same month, Bugojno and Doljani fell. As of July 30, 1993, there is combat in the Neretva Valley. In October, the AB and H took control of some villages in Vares municipality. And in November 1993, AB and H took control of Vares town. As a separate example of confusion in the Prosecution allegations, we want to point out Mostar. In their final trial brief, in para 344, they state that all of West Mostar became occupied territory, at the latest, on the 9th of May, 1993. Therefore, the Prosecutor asserts that on the day the conflict broke out in Mostar, Mostar became occupied territory. We wanted to indicate some undisputed facts to you. The conflict between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina began in Mostar on the 9th of May, 1993. Municipal HVO government, with Jadran Topic at the helm, was established in May 1992, and was not changed on the 9th of May, 1993. Herceg-Bosna central bodies were established in April and May 1992, and their authority in Mostar was not changed on the 9th of May, 1993. On the 9th of May, there was no change in terms of authorities in Western Mostar. On the 30th of June, an all-out war broke out in Mostar, lasting until the Washington Agreements were signed. Our conclusion, therefore, is unambiguous. Facts disprove Prosecution's allegations about occupation in Mostar as of 9 May 1993 onwards. A few words about occupation state of administration, given that both General Praljak and General Petkovic are charged as occupational governors. The system of administration on an occupied territory was discussed in numerous sources, and we will quote one, for example, the Benvenisti "International Law of Occupation." It is stated that in occupied territory, there can be a system of military administration or a civil one, or a mixture of both. In the manual of the UK Ministry of Defence, it is stated that in an occupied area, a military or civil government may be established. Therefore, it is asserted that the system in an occupied territory may be a civilian, a military, or a mixed one. A system of authority in a specific area is a matter of fact which needs to be proven beyond any reasonable doubt by the Prosecution. If we completely disregard the fact that Herceg-Bosna was not an occupied part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we should deal briefly with the system of administration in Herceg-Bosna as pleaded by the Prosecution. They state that civilian authorities existed in Herceg-Bosna, such as the Presidency, presidents, government, ministries, civil and military judiciary, and civil and military police. The Prosecution asserts that there was civilian control over the military. In parts of their final brief concerning responsibility of government officials, it is stated that the system of control in Herceg-Bosna was a civilian one, as asserted in para 361 of the final trial brief. Therefore, the Prosecutor does not at all assert that a military commander was tasked with running Herceg-Bosna. The Prosecutor knows and asserts that civilian authorities ran the area. We wanted to point out, Your Honours, that the Prosecution incorrectly interprets the duties of occupying commanders. Let us look yet again at paragraph 324 of their final trial brief. Petkovic and Praljak, in their respective periods and mandates, were, according to the OTP, responsible for the commission of crimes committed against civilians, irrespective of their knowledge, ignorance, measures undertaken, and all other circumstances. Namely, with the exception of this paragraph in this case, there is not a single Prosecution submission which defined differently the responsibility of occupying commanders, simply because there were no such assertions made up to that point. In order to interpret the duties of occupying commanders in this way, one would need a sound basis in international humanitarian law, which does not exist. We prepared a few excerpts from the High Command case for you, Your Honours, which we wanted to present to you in order to show the following: that the occupying commander is the commander entrusted with executive authorities. If you look at this first excerpt, you can clearly see that the phrase "endowed with executive power" is mentioned. Therefore, a military commander lacks executive power unless specifically tasked with it. The second excerpt indicates the knowledge and information at the disposal of the commander about crimes committed and that he must have known in order to be culpable. The third excerpt speaks of executive authorities which have to be endowed -- delegated to the commander. The next excerpt speaks of the lack of general presumption of the commander's knowledge about the crimes; that is to say, the burden of proof is with the Prosecution in order to prove that the occupying commander had the requisite knowledge. In the fifth excerpt, we wanted to show you a part of a judgement which has to do with the von Leeb. I hope I have pronounced that properly. I quote: "We are, therefore, unable to find from the evidence submitted that the defendant, von Leeb case. I hope I pronounced that properly. I quote: "We are therefore unable to find from the evidence submitted that the defendant, von Leeb, had knowledge of the murder of civilians within his area by the Einsatzgruppen or acquiesced in such activities. "Nor is it established from the evidence that the defendant participated in the recruitment of slave labour from the Reich." Therefore, the responsibility of an occupying commander is not presumed. It must be proven. The last excerpt from the High Command case is something of interest for these proceedings, because it has to do with the siege of Leningrad. If any of us heard of any horrific sieges throughout human history, it would probably be those who heard of Leningrad, and the conclusion is as follows: We are sorry to say that the law is as such, but that no crime was committed in the case of the siege of Leningrad. I wanted to conclude this part by saying that Herceg-Bosna was not an occupied part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in our view. Therefore, we can conclude the following: Not every military commander on the occupied territory is a military governor or a commanding general. A commanding general in an occupied territory is that commander which was appointed governor, entrusted with administrative tasks and those of the executive authorities. Duties and responsibilities of a particular military commander within an occupied territory is a question of fact, and the Prosecution has to prove them beyond reasonable doubt. The criminal responsibility of occupying commanders is a form of command responsibility defined in Article 7(3) of the Statute. The Prosecution proved that the government in Bosnia and Herzegovina was a civilian one and the civil had control over the military. We wanted to reiterate yet again that this does not include operational command. The Petkovic Defence was clear on the point. Jadranko Prlic, as the HVO government president, did not issue orders to the military, in terms of operational orders. Bruno Stojic, as the minister of defence, never issued an order to General Petkovic to undertake a specific combat operation or activity by any unit of the HVO. We'd like to close this topic of occupational governors by having said this with regard to General Petkovic. Your Honours, is this a suitable time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This will be our last break of 20 minutes for the day. Thank you. Stand up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to continue with this hearing. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I know that it is tedious to listen to a single person for such an extended period of time, but this was the only way we could organise ourselves. To continue with our closing arguments, we'll briefly look at the closing arguments of the Praljak Defence. It was not our intention to respond to the final briefs and closing arguments of other Defences, believing that in the past five years we have had ample opportunity to say everything we deemed relevant. However, one assertion was made during the closing argument by General Praljak's counsel, and it was that assertion which drove us to change our previous decision. Let us have a look at what it actually is. It has to do with something that was stated at page 52484 and 52485, with regard to document P1236. It is a -- P1163, which is under seal. I would like to ask that it not be broadcast, and I will strive not to refer directly to the contents of the document, itself. General Praljak's counsel said as follows: [In English] "In the oral presentation, the Prosecutor referred to document P1163, page 3, indicating that General Praljak was in Mostar before he came to Prozor, and that he issued an order to Miro Andric. The Prosecutor found his conclusion on the fact that the general is mentioned in the text of this document. However, the general's name is not mentioned. But, in any case, the Prosecution concludes that the general is Slobodan Praljak and that he was the one who issued the order in Mostar because General Petkovic was in Geneva. However, on the 15th and 16th of January, 1993, General Petkovic was not in Geneva." [Interpretation] End of quote. There is reference made to a document in the text that follows, confirming that Milivoj Petkovic was in Mostar in the course of those few days. The counsel concluded by saying: [In English] "So the Prosecution erroneously refers to this document so that the Trial Chamber would also draw a wrong conclusion from it." [Interpretation] End of quote. Given that this is a direct suggestion that the message Andric mentioned in document P1162 is a message from his commander, who was a general based in Mostar, and that this document refers to General Petkovic, allegedly, it is this Defence that wishes to draw your attention to the following: The assertion in this document about a general in Mostar cannot be in regard to -- with regard to General Petkovic because General Petkovic at that point in time was not a general. At that point in time, he was a brigadier, which can be seen in all the documents he issued whereby he stipulates his military rank. We prepared one such document, which is P1322, Petkovic's order of the 27th of January, 1993. The contents are unimportant at this point in time. We can see, however, that in January 1993, Milivoj Petkovic was a brigadier. Therefore, a general in Mostar referred to in the document could not have been Milivoj Petkovic. We would like to draw your attention to a paragraph in the Praljak Defence final brief, which is paragraph 406, which says, I quote: [In English] "Slobodan Praljak was not, prior to action taken by the HVO (including units Maturice and Apostoli from Kiseljak), informed about assessment of Ivica Rajic, nor was he informed which action the HVO forces are taking. When the accused did receive the information (3D00823) of Ivica Rajic on 23rd October 1993, it was later that day or in the evening. After receiving this information, the accused Praljak reacted promptly. On the same day at 1110 hours, he sent a message to Petkovic, advising him to settle down the situation in Vares without mercy to anyone and to find the men who are up to time and task. It must be noted that Praljak did not order Petkovic to do anything. He merely offered him an advice. If Praljak, as the commander of General Staff, considered it necessary, he would surely say so. He would surely write down the word 'order.' It is logical that, instead, Praljak chose to offer only a piece of advice or suggestion to Petkovic because Petkovic was on the field. He could easily obtain any additional information needed for proper decisions, and Petkovic was commander of the area (de jure and de facto) pursuant to the previously issued orders." [Interpretation] End of quote. What I would like to draw the Bench's attention to is the allegation that Petkovic then was the de jure and de facto commander of the area pursuant to previously issued orders. These orders -- or, rather, documents are mentioned in footnote 550. In the right-hand column of this table, you can see the documents cited in that footnote. The first document is 3D1161. That's an order of General Slobodan Praljak on the organisation of duty operations shifts in the Main Staff. And the second document is 3D2756, also General Praljak's order about the composition of the duty operative team from the 22nd until the 29th of October, 1993. The third document is an order issued by General Petkovic on 4 November 1993 about the area around Kiseljak. The document number is P6408. Therefore, Your Honours, the Praljak defence that pursuant to these orders about duty shifts in the Main Staff, General Petkovic had de jure commander's powers in Central Bosnia, we will not comment on those allegations, but we leave it to you to assess its validity based on the documents as cited in the footnote. Now we will deal with analysing the Prosecution's closing arguments, which was presented by my learned friend Ms. West and partly by my learned friend Mr. Scott. Ms. West, as you can see here, tried to put it to us that the Petkovic Defence claims that Petkovic never took part in a meeting with President Tudjman, but the OTP have found out that he did, after all, attend a meeting with President Tudjman on the 5th of November, 1993, in Split. Let us take a look at the Petkovic final brief about that meeting with President Tudjman in Split. The Petkovic Defence mentions it in at least three paragraphs. These paragraphs are 464, 532 and 537. The Prosecution tried to put it wrongly to the Trial Chamber that the Petkovic Defence tried to hide our client's participation in the meeting on the 5th of April, 1993, meeting in Split, where President Tudjman was. They tried to show that Mr. Petkovic attended various meetings about the strategy in Herceg-Bosna and political issues, and so the OTP, on transcript pages 52013 and the following, states that Petkovic did participate in at least two very important meetings. They mention a meeting in Zagreb, in Tudjman's office, in April 1993. We would like to point it out to you, Your Honours, what is said in the annex of the Petkovic final brief, Annex 1, page 2, that is, where you see excerpts from decisions that were signed or excerpts from the joint statement and its annexes as signed at the meeting in Zagreb on 25 April 1993. This is a joint statement signed by Izetbegovic, Boban and Tudjman, and the supplement -- or the military supplement to the joint statement, signed by Halilovic and Petkovic. This document has been shown in this courtroom by the Petkovic Defence zillions of times, and we will show it yet again in our closing arguments. For the time being, I'll say this was a meeting of the Muslim and Croatian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in President Tudjman's office, in the presence of the international community, so this is not a meeting of Croatian politicians who discussed a strategy of whatever sort or other things in Herceg-Bosna, as the Prosecution wishes to present it. We do consider this meeting as one of the most important events, and it really has nothing to do with any agreements about criminal objectives of Herceg-Bosna. On transcript page 52016, it says that the Petkovic Defence does not mention his report for 1992; it only mentions it in its annex. And they say that the report was allegedly issued by Petkovic. Your Honours, please take a look at the excerpt that you'll see in this table on your screens, and you will see that the documents allegedly issued by Petkovic in this annex of ours are marked red. The report for 1997 [as interpreted], P907, is under item 1, and you see that it is not mentioned -- it is not marked red. This report was used by our Defence many times, and we used it in our closing argument, and we will use it again because we consider it extremely important. We would like to point it out that the OTP falsely puts it to the Trial Chamber that the Petkovic Defence wishes to hide something or that it wrongly qualifies any document issued by Petkovic. On page 52027, we see the Prosecution's claim: "Petkovic claims that the brigade commanders did not report to him ..." Your Honours, among other things, we would like to draw your attention to paragraph 70 of the Petkovic Defence final brief, where it says clearly that the commander of the Main Staff was superior to a brigade commander and other military commanders in all issues regarding combat. We have shown many reports that military commanders sent to both Mr. Petkovic and the Main Staff, so that General Petkovic never renounced the brigade commanders of the HVO or other military commanders. What we have clearly pointed out to the Trial Chamber in these five years is the following: that the chief of Main Staff had no authority over the Convicts Battalion and that the chief of Main Staff had no authority over the military police or the civilian police, except where they were re-subordinated to the Main Staff or any military commander. The following allegation we want to comment upon is mentioned on transcript page 52028. It is about documents that define the tasks of the Main Staff. Ms. West said that the arguments of the Petkovic Defence refer to only two HVO pieces of legislation, and the stress was on "only two." What we wish to say is that it's true, only two, for the simple reason that there are no more. There were only two. So if you want to see what the duties of the chief of Main Staff were under the law, what you will have to consult are these very two pieces of legislation. By this allegation, the Prosecution falsely implied the existence of any other laws or regulations which the Petkovic Defence consciously omitted. That is why we want to state clearly and unambiguously that these two pieces of legislation are the ones that set out the authority of the Main Staff. On transcript page 52029, developing this thesis about only two pieces of legislation, Ms. West says that -- mentions exercise in linguistic gymnastics and mentions P289 and P586, and then she says, I quote: [In English] "The reason I am not going to do the analysis here is this: No matter what these documents say about Petkovic's competence as chief of the Main Staff, the Trial Chamber must look to what happened in fact, what happened on the ground, to see the real picture." [Interpretation] End of quote. In the right-hand column, Your Honours, we show excerpts from the documents I mentioned, so you can see for yourselves what they say and determine what the legal duties and obligations of the chief of Main Staff of the HVO were. What we wish to comment on now is the appeal of the Prosecution to the Trial Chamber not to heed laws and regulations, but instead to focus on the events on the ground. We would like to say to you that both matter, laws and regulations, on the one hand, and the situation on the ground, on the other. The appeal to disregard laws and regulations and focus only on events on the ground surprises us because, based on our analysis of all the laws and regulations, this trial is actually a trial for commission by omission. Commission by omission and aiding by abetting by omission are the very crux of these proceedings. To assess responsibility under these headings, you must determine the legal obligation to act, and that can only be determined by looking at laws and regulations. We cannot sentence somebody for omission and only determine the facts about what he did, and a precise analysis of the laws and regulations of Herceg-Bosna is a precondition for a fair verdict. That is why we dealt extensively with laws and regulations in our defence and attempted to give our opinion about what the laws and regulations of Herceg-Bosna say about the duty of the chief of Main Staff to do or omit to do something. I believe that you will also analyse these laws and regulations and draw your conclusions from them. We would also like to stress something else in this context; namely, that we never contested the position of the chief of Main Staff in the operative chain of command, and I stress the word "operative," because this operative chain of command has to do with combat activities. What we have alleged in these proceedings and tried to prove is that the chief of Main Staff was not in the chain of command or the chain of subordination for regular tasks of the military police, the SIS, and other non-combat activities, from the remit of individual bodies of Herceg-Bosna. We also attempted to show that the Main Staff had no authority over detention centres. Whether or not we have been successful in that respect is up to you to decide, Your Honours. The following submission of the Prosecution we would like to comment on is recorded on page 52031 of the transcript. Ms. West said, I quote: [In English] "Mr. Scott mentioned this chart as well, and it's clearly contrary to the Defence position that Petkovic was not in command and control of the armed forces." [Interpretation] End of quote. I must admit, Your Honours, that after this allegation put forward by Ms. West, General Petkovic asked me, What did you write in your final brief for the Prosecutor to say this? Please take a look at the schematic on the right-hand side. This is also a Defence document of the Petkovic Defence, 4D618. This document was used by General Petkovic when he was examined in the Blaskic case, so it was used some 10 years ago or so, and we wanted it to be an exhibit in this trial because it shows what General Petkovic said in another trial without knowing that he would be -- he would stand trial here one day. And it is important information that the Convicts Battalion is not in the system of responsibility of the Main Staff. This was a chart that we used during our case. And based on it, we examined many of our own witnesses and other witnesses, and Generals Petkovic and Praljak also testified about it. Let me, therefore, repeat once more. It is uncontested that the chief of Main Staff was part of the chain of command and in exactly the manner as stated by the witnesses of the Petkovic Defence, as we have mentioned it in our final brief. Further on, on transcript page 52039, the Prosecutor referred to paragraph 212 in the Petkovic Defence final brief and said -- actually, they quoted one part of our paragraph 212 and then they said: [In English] "Now the brief does not give any citation for this assertion that the government only is responsible and not anyone else, and there is no source listed." [Interpretation] Your Honours, look at the entire paragraph 212 of the Petkovic Defence final brief, and you will see that there is a footnote there, footnote 410. Furthermore, look at the documents referred to in that footnote, in footnote 410. We have prepared parts of the regulations that we referred to when we compiled paragraph 212 of our final brief. Allow me to read what we wrote there. In annex to the 1907 Hague Convention, it is said, and I quote: [In English] "Prisoners of war are in the power of the hostile government, but not of the individuals who captured them. "Article 7: The government into whose hands prisoners of war had faller is charged with their maintenance. "Article 14: An inquiry officer for prisoners of war is instituted on the commencement of hostilities in each of the belligerent states and, when necessary, in neutral countries which have received belligerence in their territory. It is the function of this office to reply to all inquiries about the prisoners. It received from the various services concerned full information respecting internment and transfers, releases on parole, exchanges, escapes, admissions into hospitals, deaths, as well as other information necessary to enable it to make out and keep up to date an individual return for each prisoner of war." [Interpretation] The second document that we referred to in the footnote is the Geneva Convention III. I quote: [In English] "Article 12: Prisoners of war are in the hands of the enemy power, but not of the individuals or military units who have captured them." [Interpretation] The commentary of the International Committee of the Red Cross, the first sentence reads, I quote: [In English] "The logical consequence is that prisoners of war are not in the power of the individuals or military units who have captured them. They are in the hands of the state itself over which these individuals or military units are only the agents. The present provision, which formally establishes this principle, reproduces the text of Article 2, paragraph 1, of the 1929 Convention, which, in turn, was derived from Article 4, paragraph 1, of The Hague Regulations of 1907." [Interpretation] We would also like to point to a completely erroneous conclusion by my learned friend from the Prosecution. She claims that the Petkovic Defence claimed that only the government was responsible for the treatment of POWs. There is no such claim in our final argument. Within that context, it might be of some interest to remind everybody that Mr. Scott arrived at a completely different conclusion, based on our final brief. On the one hand, Ms. West concludes that only the government was responsible, whereas Mr. Scott concluded that the Petkovic Defence considered the Ministry of Defence and the military police as persons responsible for the treatment of prisoners of war in detention centres. A large part of the closing argument of our learned friend from the Prosecution was dedicated to artillery fire and the responsibilities of those responsible for the artillery, and that is recorded on pages T-52061 and P52064 [as interpreted]. Those assertions, briefly, concern the fact that the Main Staff had responsibilities over the artillery, that Milivoj Petkovic, as the chief of the Main Staff, had full authority over the artillery, and that he used those authorities, that he exercised his rights. We shall deal with the part of the documents that were of some relevance for this topic. The first one is P04131. This is an order issued on the 12th of August, 1993, about the changes in the chain of command which were to be implemented when General Praljak took over the command of the Main Staff. Under item 2, you will see entirely that it was decided for the Rocket Battalion to be subordinated directly to the Main Staff. General Praljak testified at great length about that. He explained why the artillery fire was being centralised by this decision. Other witnesses confirmed that in their testimonies. Among them was also Petkovic's witness, Maric. It is very clear in the document that up to that moment, the Rocket Regiment was never subordinated to the Main Staff. If the Rocket Regiment had ever been subordinated to the Main Staff, General Praljak would have never issued an order to this effect, it would have been unnecessary. Therefore, it is completely erroneous to conclude that Milivoj Petkovic, as the chief of the Main Staff, had authorities that did not exist before the 12th of August, 1993, and that person number 1 of the Main Staff never had. Let's look at the following document, which is P6950. Towards the end of November, 1993, the commander of the South-East Herzegovina OZ, Mr. Miljenko Lasic, sent a request to the chief of the Main Staff, Ante Roso, for the Rocket Regiment to be returned under the authority of the OZ, which used to be the South-East Herzegovina OG. On the 1st of December, 1993, document P6990 was sent by the chief of Main Staff, Ante Roso, and by that order he re-subordinated the Rocket Regiment to the Military District of Mostar until further proceedings. It arises unambiguously from these documents that the Main Staff at the time, and Milivoj Petkovic was its chief, was not in command of the Rocket Regiment. There is no reason whatsoever not to establish very clearly what happened and what the sequence of events was. We will be able to do that if we analyse all of the documents and if we see what the relationship between those documents is. Furthermore, in their closing argument, on page 52064, the Prosecutor stated that one document, dated 22nd July, showed that General Petkovic, prior to leaving his office as the chief of the Main Staff, had requested data on artillery, and this, according to them, was a clear suggestion that there was a combat being prepared. As you can see from the quote, the document has been admitted under P343. And now let's look at the document on the right-hand side. The document was indeed issued on the 22nd of July, but not in 1993, as has been suggested by the Prosecutor, but rather in 1992. In other words, that document was issued in mid-1992, when the Main Staff of the HVO still didn't have a clue what kind of artillery pieces were in the hands of their units on the ground, but when the Main Staff tried to gather information as to what kind of artillery power the HVO had at its disposal. The Prosecution completely erroneously suggested to the Trial Chamber that Petkovic did something immediately around the time when he left his position. They did that by missing the date of the document by merely a year. Your Honours, I would like to point out to one part of the closing argument delivered by my learned friend Mr. Scott that refers to General Petkovic. My learned friend Mr. Scott, inter alia, on page P51848, mentioned a document, 35377, that the document was issued by General Petkovic, and that document says, inter alia -- I'm repeating the document number -- first the page number, P51848 and then the document number P377. P377 is the document number, and the page number is correct, yes. Very well. My learned friend Mr. Scott quoted one part of the order dated 10 August 1992, where it says, and I quote: [In English] "Use all available HVO civilian and military police forces to prevent any military units, other than the HVO, from entering your area of responsibility. This is solely HVO territory. None others are welcome. None others will be accepted. You are to advise the staff on the presence of any unit other than the HVO." [Interpretation] On the right-hand side of this page, Your Honours, we are providing you with the integral text of this order issued by Petkovic, and we would like to draw your attention to the fact that this order was sent to the following cities: Livno, Tomislavgrad, Posusje, Siroki Brijeg, Mostar, Capljina, Ljubuski and Citluk. At that moment in the month of August 1992, BiH Army units existed only in the territory of Mostar. As for the other municipalities, there were no HVO units there. And if you -- I apologise. There were no BiH Army units there. I thank my colleague for the intervention. So the only municipality where a BiH Army unit existed was Mostar; nowhere else. That fact would have been reasonable grounds to ask ourselves as to what hid behind the order issued by Brigadier Petkovic. Was there another reason, and not what was suggested to us by the Prosecutor? Why did General Petkovic put a ban on the entry of BiH Army units? We believe that the answer lies in P391. This is the minutes of the HZ-HB session which was held on the 14th of August, 1992, in Grude. If we look at the last lines of the excerpt, we will see that a warning was issued at the meeting to the effect that the HVO was privy to the information that the HOS were poised to take over in Ljubuski, Capljina, and other municipalities in that part of Herzegovina. Within that context, Petkovic's order issued in August 1992 cannot be interpreted in any other way but as an order that is relative to the HOS and not to the BiH Army. And now, Your Honours, with regard to this type of interpretation of documents, and drawing conclusions either based on the erroneous interpretation of entire documents or parts thereof, I would like to remind you that all Defence teams, those who were delivering their arguments before me, invited the Trial Chamber to carefully analyse each and every document and to analyse their context. Otherwise, if you don't do that, by combining selected parts of documents, irrespective of the date when they were created, irrespective of the participants and the context, any kind of picture could be created, as is indeed possible according to the mosaic theory. If you take parts of certain documents and put them together, you can get whatever you wish. However, proper reading of documents, proper reading of context, can bring us closer to the truth. And now, Your Honours, we will embark on our commentary of the Prosecutor's final brief, although I believe that whatever I have done so far is pretty tiring, so if you don't mind, if it's all the same to you, I don't mind continuing tomorrow instead of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue now. We still have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's start analysing the Prosecutor's final trial brief. In paragraph 3 of its final trial brief, the Prosecutor says: [In English] "This is especially true of the testimony of the accused Praljak and Petkovic, who lied repeatedly when they were not evading questions on important issues. Their self-serving testimony is entitled to little weight." [Interpretation] The Prosecutor, therefore, claims about General Praljak and about General Petkovic that they both lied. Of course, I'm going to provide comments only with regard to the parts dealing with General Petkovic. Further on, the Prosecution doesn't give us a single example to corroborate their claim that General Petkovic lied in his testimony. We believe that such a claim in a final brief is inappropriate, and if anybody in -- if nobody in the courtroom, when examining their witnesses, was not able to prove that they are lying, that it is inappropriate for them to claim something like that in their final brief. We also believe that it is an inappropriate expression, when we look at paragraph 867 of the Prosecution's final trial brief, where it says, inter alia, and I quote: [In English] "The meaning couldn't be clearer, and Petkovic's assertions are comical, at best, and dishonest, at worst." [Interpretation] We also believe it to be completely inappropriate to state what was stated in para 868, that Petkovic was trying to convey something through Praljak. General Praljak spoke on his behalf, much as General Petkovic did, as well as all the other participants of the meeting referred to in that paragraph. We won't comment upon this mode of expression, but we merely wanted to note that it is entirely inappropriate as part of a final trial brief in proceedings such as this. In several paragraphs in their final trial brief, the OTP referred to document P279 let's look at paragraph 11 for that purpose. It is stated as follows for General Petkovic: [In English] "The accused intended to achieve Croat control over Herceg-Bosna through deportation and forcible transfer, together forcible displacement. As early as June 1992, Petkovic cited the need to establish Croatian rule over all municipalities." [Interpretation] In paragraph 861, this speech is mentioned as well, as well as in 864. I must admit that while reading the OTP final brief, my impression was that there was a number of speeches or contributions, and only then I realised that the Prosecutor kept going back to one single document. So let's look at that document together. It is P279. You are familiar with it, Your Honours, since, on the basis of that document, you put many questions to General Petkovic. Let's look at how the document opens. I quote: [In English] "General, gentlemen of municipal leadership and commanders of HVO units, today we shall analyse current operative and tactical situation, further intentions and tasks, and consider all the problems that we have and are confronted with that need urgent solutions. Agenda of this meeting has been created to serve that purpose. We have to give proper answers to the questions and problems that we shall talk about. (Inform about the agenda.)" [Interpretation] Based on this introductory part of the document, one concludes that it is completely unambiguous that this is not a written report, but a draft speech that was supposed to be held at a meeting which was supposed to be attended by a general. It was General Bobetko. In attendance, there should also have been members of municipal authorities and commanders of certain areas. The first and basic question to put is this: If we realise that a document is a draft speech, we must ask ourselves whether it was ever held or not, because if it had not been, then there is no actus reus, there is no activity which would initiate anything. The Prosecutor did not offer a single piece of evidence that General Petkovic indeed made this speech, as drafted in this document. On the other hand, General Petkovic's Defence provided the following proof: General Petkovic explained what took part at the meeting. He also said that he never made the speech, and that rather, standing in front of a map, he explained the situation in the field. This was at transcript page 49351, 49351 to 49353. Our witness, General Beneta, confirmed that General Petkovic spoke in front of the map, addressing directly those in attendance while he was not reading out of anything. General Beneta's testimony is at transcript page 46606 to 46607. With regard to this document, Your Honours, we also wish to draw your attention to one part of it that you can see on the screen, which contains a list of municipalities whose representatives were supposed to have attended the meeting. Let's have a look at what those municipalities were: Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, Citluk, Ljubuski, Capljina, Grude, Stolac, Neum, and Ravno. If you recall the testimonies of General Beneta and of Bozo Pavlovic, as well as of General Praljak and General Petkovic, you will see that in June 1992, it was precisely this area of Bosnia and Herzegovina that had been liberated and taken over from the JNA and the Serb forces, and that in Stolac there was an attempt to organise civilian authorities. As for the other municipalities in question, they already had civilian authorities in place; that is to say, all of the municipalities, save for Mostar and Stolac, were predominantly populated by Croats. Hence, there were no changes in the authorities of those municipalities. If we take another look at the document, we see that neither in its introductory part, nor anywhere else, we have the registry file number. We do not believe this is a decisive piece of evidence, but it's at least an indication that the document had never received an official filing number. That is why we wish to reiterate the following concerning this document: This speech was never made. Concerning this speech, there is no actus reus, and the Petkovic Defence, however, does not deny that this document is important to ascertain Petkovic's mens rea. We do not shy away from it, and we will address it specifically in the continuation of our closing argument. What we are trying to stress for the time being is that this is not an anti-Muslim speech, as the Prosecutor would have you believe, and we will prove that by showing you a number of other documents and reports issued by Petkovic, at the time and later, which clearly and unambiguously confirm that Petkovic did not have any anti-Muslim intentions and that the mention of Croatian rules did not mean the denigration of Muslims. In order to begin with that exercise, I wanted to show you first 4D830. Basically, it is the same document as P907, the report on Petkovic's work in 1992. In general conclusions, General Petkovic states as follows: "At this moment in time, HVO forces successfully hold on to 90 per cent of the territory envisaged as the territory of Herceg-Bosna." In item 7, he states that: "HVO forces, despite numerous obstacles and problems, hold 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina under their control." Your Honours, we wanted to draw your attention to this part of the report. This sentence makes it clear that General Petkovic believed that the free part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was also that part which was held by BH Army at the time. The sentence following that is -- given that I have this document in English, I'll read it out in English: [In English] "By organising its own armed forces in the territory of HZ-HB, Croatian people defended themselves and majority of Muslims." [Interpretation] Therefore, General Petkovic in the report states that the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna defended the Croatian people and most Muslims. Therefore, there was no doubt in General Petkovic's mind that the HVO forces are the forces defending the Croatian and Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Based on this small portion of this document, we can see that General Petkovic believed the HVO capable of defending and keeping under control a certain part of territory, meaning that neither General Petkovic nor anyone else in the Main Staff or in the HVO had planned any offensive operations. It is also a fact that it is stated therein that 90 per cent of the territory was under control of the authorities of Herceg-Bosna. It clearly indicates that the HVO had no offensive plans and that there were no preparations under way to attack the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They did not wish to expand the territory that had already been under control of the authorities of Herceg-Bosna by use of arms. Your Honours, this brings us to the next large topic. Hence, I suggest that we continue tomorrow, since we only have five minutes left, by your leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wanted to tell you that you have one and a half hours left for tomorrow, one and a half hours. Actually, it is one hour and thirty-five minutes. Therefore, we continue with your argument tomorrow, following which we have Mr. Coric's Defence. I wish you a good evening. And as you know, we continue tomorrow at 2.15 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of February, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.54 p.m.,
